newsitem.title: INDIA: High domestic prices hit Indian sugar exports.
newsitem.headline: High domestic prices hit Indian sugar exports.

text.p: High domestic prices and an anticipated dip in output will substantially cut India's sugar exports in the 1996/97 (October-September) season despite the end of trade controls, officials said on Thursday.
"There are hardly any exports (left)," S.L. Jain, director-general of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), told Reuters.
In January the government ended the Indian Sugar and General Industry Export-Import Corp's export monopoly. ISGIEC is a private corporation set up by the sugar milling industry.

The decision was considered an important step towards freeing the sugar industry from a decades-old system of licensing, pricing and distribution geared to balance the interests of producers and consumers.
"Indian sugar exports have come to a trickle because they are not viable. World prices are much lower," said Yatin Wadhwana, an official in a leading Delhi sugar export firm.
Food Ministry officials said the government had authorised the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) to export 250,000 tonnes of sugar after deregulation.
"Out of these, only 25,000 tonnes of sugar have been exported, by rail to Pakistan," Jain said.
APEDA officials said that out of its authorised quota, APEDA issued licences for the export of 162,985 tonnes of sugar, out of which 36,000 tonnes have been physically exported.
India had exported about 1.1 million tonnes until December 1996 when the government deregulated sugar exports, Food Ministry officials said.

Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra said earlier this week sugar output in 1996/97 was expected to dip to 13 million tonnes from 16.5 million in 1995/96 but the situation would be comfortable due to excess carry-over stocks.

Mishra said the output was expected to decline due to a fall in area under the crop in the current season. The acreage has fallen because farmers were discouraged by delayed payment for the previous season's sugarcane output.
"The situation is quite comfortable. We have enough stocks," M.S. Bhatia, economic advisor in the Agriculture Ministry, told Reuters.
A senior Food Ministry official said: "As of today we have stocks of 12 million tonnes, which is slightly less than that of one year's requirement."
India entered the 1996/97 season with carry-over stocks of eight million tonnes.
Industry and state officials officials said domestic demand in the current season was expected to be about 14 million tonnes compared with estimated output of 13 million.
"Local prices will therefore remain high and we have to eat at least one million tonnes from carry-over stocks," Wadhwana said.
Jain said the situation would be comfortable in the 1997/98 season, with the year starting with a surplus stock of seven million tonnes.
